html:
The Battle of Poltava was fought on 8 July 1709 (27 June in the old Russian calendar) outside the town of Poltava in central Ukraine. The Russian army of Tsar Peter the Great destroyed the Swedish army of King Charles XII.

It was the turning point of the Great Northern War, in which Russia and its allies fought Sweden for control of the Baltic. Charles invaded Russia in 1708. The Russians burned the land in front of him, so he turned south into Ukraine to join the Cossack leader Ivan Mazepa. A very cold winter and the loss of a supply column weakened his army. In 1709 he besieged Poltava. Peter came with about 42,000 men and many more guns, and built a fortified camp. Charles, wounded in the foot, sent about 17,000 men to attack it. They were shot down, and the survivors surrendered three days later at the Dnieper. Charles fled to the Ottoman Empire.

Sweden's time as a great power was over. Russia took the Baltic coast, where Peter was building Saint Petersburg, and became the leading power of northern Europe. Mazepa's defeat also ended the Cossack hope of a Ukraine free of Moscow.
